conventional_description:
In Western medicine, constipation is defined as having fewer than three bowel movements per week, with stools that are often hard, dry, and difficult to pass. It may also involve a sensation of incomplete evacuation or needing to strain. The condition is extremely common, affecting up to 20% of the population, and is more frequent in women and older adults.
Diagnosis is usually based on symptom criteria such as the Rome IV guidelines, and may include a physical exam and sometimes imaging to rule out obstruction or other underlying disorders.
Typical causes include a low-fiber diet, inadequate fluid intake, lack of physical activity, certain medications, and ignoring the urge to go. In some cases, constipation is linked to conditions like irritable bowel syndrome, hypothyroidism, or neurological disorders. Conventional treatment focuses on relieving the immediate symptom and addressing lifestyle factors.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment begins with lifestyle changes: increasing dietary fiber, drinking more water, and regular exercise. Over-the-counter remedies include bulk-forming laxatives (psyllium), osmotic laxatives (polyethylene glycol, lactulose), and stool softeners (docusate). For more stubborn cases, stimulant laxatives (bisacodyl, senna) may be used short-term. Prescription medications such as lubiprostone or linaclotide are available for chronic idiopathic constipation. In severe cases, biofeedback therapy or surgery may be considered.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the Large Intestine is responsible for receiving waste from the Small Intestine, absorbing remaining fluids, and propelling stool downward for elimination. This process depends on two things: enough Qi to push, and enough moisture to lubricate. When either is lacking, constipation results. But the Large Intestine doesn't work in isolation - it relies on the Spleen and Stomach for Qi production, the Liver for smooth movement, and the Kidneys for fluid balance.
The Spleen-Stomach system is the engine of digestion. They transform food into Qi and send it downward. If Spleen Qi is weak, the Large Intestine lacks the energy to move stool effectively - even if the stool is soft, you may strain and feel exhausted afterwards. This is the Qi Deficiency pattern.
If the Stomach accumulates excess heat (from spicy food, stress, or infection), that heat dries up intestinal fluids, creating hard, dry, pebble-like stools - the Excess-Heat pattern.
The Liver governs the free flow of Qi throughout the body. Emotional stress, frustration, or prolonged sitting can cause Liver Qi to stagnate, which then disrupts the downward movement of the Large Intestine. This leads to constipation that comes and goes with stress, often accompanied by bloating and belching - the Liver Qi Stagnation pattern.
Moisture is equally critical. Blood and Yin fluids lubricate the intestines. When Blood is deficient (common after childbirth, heavy periods, or in the elderly), the bowel becomes dry and stools harden - the Blood Deficiency pattern. When Yin fluids are depleted (from chronic illness, overwork, or aging), the same dryness occurs but with signs of heat like night sweats - the Yin Deficiency pattern.
Even after a high fever or excessive sweating, body fluids can be so depleted that the Large Intestine simply dries out - the Large Intestine Dryness pattern.
So the same Western diagnosis of constipation can stem from heat, stagnation, or various deficiencies. TCM doesn't just ask if you're constipated; it asks what the stool looks like, how it feels to pass, and what else is happening in your body - thirst, energy, emotional state, tongue appearance, and pulse quality. This detailed differentiation allows treatment to target the root cause, not just force a bowel movement.
classical_quote: 「阳明病，谵语，有潮热，反不能食者，胃中必有燥屎五六枚也，宜大承气汤下之。」

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first asks about the stool itself. If it is dry, hard, and pellet-like, with a feeling of heat in the abdomen, thirst, and a yellow tongue coating, the picture points toward Excess-Heat. A rapid, full pulse confirms that heat is drying up fluids in the intestines, making the stool difficult to pass.
When a person feels the urge to go but has to strain and sweat, and the stool may not even be very dry, the practitioner suspects Qi Deficiency. The key question is whether fatigue and shortness of breath accompany the effort. A pale tongue and a weak, thready pulse reveal that the propulsive force of the Large Intestine is too weak to move the stool.
Dry stools paired with a dull complexion, dizziness, or brittle nails suggest Blood Deficiency. This pattern often appears after childbirth or in the elderly. The practitioner asks about menstrual history or any blood loss, and looks for a pale tongue body and a thin, choppy pulse - signs that the body lacks the nourishment to lubricate the bowel.
If constipation comes with bloating, belching, and a tight sensation in the sides, and it flares up with emotional stress, Liver Qi Stagnation is the likely pattern. The practitioner checks for a wiry pulse and asks about mood and tension. Here the problem is not a lack of fluids or strength, but a disruption in the smooth downward flow of intestinal Qi.

patterns.symptoms: ["Hard, dry stools that are difficult to pass", "Intense thirst with craving for cold drinks", "Feeling of heat throughout the body", "Red flushed face", "Dark, scanty urine", "Restlessness and irritability"]
patterns.worse_with: Spicy, greasy, dry, or deep-fried foods, Alcohol, Hot, dry weather, Emotional stress, frustration, or anger, Overexertion, overwork, or lack of sleep
patterns.better_with: Cold drinks, Cooling foods (pears, watermelon), Cool, humid environment, Gentle exercise (like walking), Drinking plenty of water
patterns.why_this_happens: When excess heat builds up in the Stomach and Intestines, it burns off the fluids that normally keep the stool soft and easy to pass. The Large Intestine becomes dry, and the stool hardens into dry lumps that are difficult to evacuate. This heat also creates a strong thirst for cold drinks and a general feeling of being overheated.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, possibly with prickles, thick dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid (Shu) and forceful, overflowing (Hong), broad and surging.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Excess heat consumes the body's fluids, drying out the intestines. Cooling foods and drinks clear heat and generate fluids, helping to moisten the stool. Spicy, greasy foods and alcohol add more heat and further deplete fluids, worsening constipation. Stress and overwork stir up internal heat, while a cool environment and rest allow the body to cool down and preserve fluids.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat plenty of cooling, high-water-content foods like pears, watermelon, cucumber, and celery. Avoid spicy, greasy, and fried foods, as well as alcohol and coffee, which add heat and dry out the intestines. Drink water at room temperature or cool, not iced, throughout the day. Gentle daily exercise like walking helps keep the bowels moving.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen and Stomach produce the Qi that powers the intestines. When Qi is deficient, the Large Intestine lacks the strength to push stools out, even when the urge is present. This leads to straining, sweating, and exhaustion with bowel movements, and stools may be soft but still difficult to pass.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: Pale, puffy, tender body with teeth marks; thin white coating. Pulse: Empty (Xu) or weak (Ruo).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Qi deficiency means the body's vital energy is low. Rest and gentle movement conserve and generate Qi, while overexertion and stress deplete it further. Warm, cooked foods are easy to digest and support the Spleen's production of Qi; cold and raw foods tax the digestive system. Abdominal massage helps move local Qi to stimulate bowel function without draining energy.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked, easily digestible foods such as congee, soups, and steamed vegetables. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that weaken the Spleen. Gentle daily walking or tai chi can help move Qi without depleting it. Rest when tired and avoid overexertion.

patterns.why_this_happens: Blood nourishes and moistens every tissue, including the intestines. When Blood is deficient, the Large Intestine becomes like a riverbed without enough water - dry, parched, and unable to move waste smoothly. The stool loses its lubrication, becoming dry, hard, and difficult to pass. This pattern is especially common after childbirth, during prolonged illness, or in the elderly, when the body's Blood reserves are naturally low.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with thin white coating. Pulse: fine (Xi) and weak.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Overwork and postpartum states drain Blood, which is already scarce in this pattern, worsening the intestinal dryness. Raw and cold foods further injure the Spleen, the source of Blood production. Warm, nourishing meals and adequate rest support the Spleen and Stomach in building new Blood, while gentle movement encourages Qi flow - the force that moves both Blood and stool - without depleting reserves.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat small, warm, nourishing meals like congees with red dates, goji berries, and a little black sesame. Avoid raw, cold foods and excessive fasting. Gentle daily movement like walking helps Qi and Blood circulate without exhausting reserves. Prioritize rest and avoid overwork.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi throughout the body, including the downward movement of the Large Intestine. When emotional stress or frustration causes Liver Qi to stagnate, this downward movement is disrupted, leading to a sluggish or spastic bowel. The result is constipation that comes and goes with stress, often accompanied by bloating, belching, and a feeling of incomplete evacuation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: normal or slightly dark body with red or slightly purple sides, thin white coating. Pulse: wiry (弦 xián), like a taut guitar string, especially at the left middle position.

Movement and relaxation help unblock that stagnation, while warm, aromatic herbs gently encourage Qi to descend and move the stool.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Incorporate gentle daily movement like walking or yoga to keep Qi flowing. Eat mindfully and avoid rushing meals; include small amounts of peppermint, fennel, or citrus peel in your tea. Manage stress with deep breathing or meditation, as emotional tension directly tightens the bowels.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Large Intestine relies on body fluids to lubricate the passage of stool. When those fluids are depleted - often after a high fever, excessive sweating, or chronic dehydration - the bowel becomes too dry to move waste smoothly. This causes hard, pellet-like stools that are difficult to evacuate, even when the urge to go is present.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin, and dry body with cracks, especially in the center; coating is thin, dry, and slightly yellow. Pulse: fine (thin) and may feel choppy, often weaker in the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: This pattern is driven by a shortage of the fluids that moisten and lubricate the Large Intestine. Warm water and moistening foods directly replenish those fluids, while rest allows the body to conserve and rebuild Yin. Spicy foods, sweating, and dry environments drain the very fluids that are already scarce, making the stool harder and more difficult to pass.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Drink warm water throughout the day and include moistening foods like pears, honey, sesame seeds, and cooked apples. Avoid dry, crunchy snacks and limit coffee and alcohol. A humidifier in dry rooms can help, and gentle daily movement supports bowel function.

patterns.why_this_happens: Yin is the body's cooling and moistening resource. When Yin runs low, the fluids that normally lubricate the intestines dry up, leaving the stool hard and difficult to move forward. It is like a boat stranded in a riverbed that has lost its water. The systemic signs of Yin deficiency - night sweats, a dry mouth, and a sensation of heat in the palms and soles - appear alongside the constipation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red, thin body with cracks; little or no coating; dry surface. Pulse: fine (thin) and rapid.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Yin deficiency leaves the body short on cooling, moistening resources. Spicy, fried foods and hot, dry weather consume those scarce fluids, while late nights and overwork directly deplete Yin. Rest, sleep, and moistening foods help replenish Yin and gently lubricate the intestines, making stools easier to pass.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Prioritize moistening foods like pears, honey, sesame, spinach, and congee. Avoid spicy, fried, and drying foods, and keep alcohol and coffee to a minimum. Go to bed by 11 p.m. and protect your sleep; late nights are one of the fastest ways to burn through Yin.

faqs.question: Can Chinese herbs cause diarrhea?
faqs.answer: TCM formulas for constipation are designed to promote a gentle, natural bowel movement, not a sudden purge. However, if a formula is too strong for your constitution, it could cause loose stools. A qualified practitioner will adjust the dosage or herbs to avoid this. Always inform your practitioner if you experience any change in bowel habits.

faqs.question: How long does it take for Chinese herbs to work for constipation?
faqs.answer: Many people notice a difference within the first week, especially with excess patterns. However, chronic constipation due to deficiency may take 2-4 weeks to see consistent improvement, and full resolution may take a couple of months. Patience is key, as TCM aims to correct the underlying imbalance, not just stimulate a bowel movement.

faqs.question: Can I use TCM alongside my regular laxatives?
faqs.answer: Yes, but with caution. It's best to work with both your TCM practitioner and your doctor to coordinate care. Stimulant laxatives can be habit-forming, so TCM may help you reduce or eliminate them over time. Never stop prescription medications without medical guidance. Herbs that moisten the intestines (like Huo Ma Ren) are generally safe alongside osmotic laxatives, but always disclose all medications to your practitioner.

faqs.question: Is constipation always a sign of heat in TCM?
faqs.answer: No. While heat is a common cause - leading to dry, hard stools - constipation can also result from Qi deficiency (weak propulsion), Blood deficiency (dryness from lack of nourishment), or Liver Qi stagnation (stress-related). The stool's consistency and accompanying symptoms help differentiate the pattern. For example, soft stools that are hard to push out suggest Qi deficiency, not heat.

faqs.question: What foods should I avoid if I have constipation?
faqs.answer: In general, avoid drying, spicy, and greasy foods, as well as excessive cold or raw foods that can weaken the Spleen. If your pattern involves heat, also limit alcohol and coffee. If you have Qi deficiency, avoid heavy, hard-to-digest meals. A TCM practitioner can give you personalized dietary advice based on your specific pattern.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help with constipation?
faqs.answer: Yes, acupuncture can stimulate peristalsis and relax the abdominal muscles, often providing relief within a few treatments. Points like Tianshu (ST-25) and Zhigou (SJ-6) are commonly used. For chronic constipation, acupuncture is usually combined with herbal medicine for deeper and longer-lasting results.

faqs.question: Is TCM safe for constipation during pregnancy?
faqs.answer: Many TCM herbs and acupuncture points are safe during pregnancy, but some are contraindicated because they can stimulate uterine contractions. Always tell your practitioner if you are pregnant or trying to conceive. They will use only pregnancy-safe points and gentle, nourishing herbs to address constipation without risk.

faqs.question: Will my constipation come back after I stop treatment?
faqs.answer: If the underlying imbalance has been fully corrected, bowel function should remain regular. However, if old habits (diet, stress, lifestyle) return, the pattern can re-emerge. Your practitioner will guide you on long-term maintenance, including diet and self-acupressure, to prevent recurrence.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic functional constipation
research.description: A Cochrane systematic review evaluating acupuncture for chronic constipation in adults. It included 15 RCTs and concluded that acupuncture may increase bowel movement frequency compared to sham acupuncture, but the evidence was limited by small sample sizes and risk of bias.
research.periodical: Lee MS, Choi TY, Shin BC, et al. Acupuncture for chronic functional constipation. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2016, Issue 7. Art. No.: CD004117.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for functional constipation: a systematic review and meta-analysis
research.description: This meta-analysis of 28 RCTs assessed various Chinese herbal formulas for functional constipation. It found that herbal medicine significantly improved bowel movement frequency, stool consistency, and straining compared to placebo or conventional therapy, with a favorable safety profile.
research.periodical: Liu Z, Yan S, Wu J, et al. Chinese herbal medicine for functional constipation: a systematic review and meta-analysis. Journal of Ethnopharmacology 2019; 233: 34-46.

research.title: Ma Zi Ren Wan for opioid-induced constipation in patients with cancer: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: A randomized controlled trial testing Ma Zi Ren Wan against a placebo in cancer patients with opioid-induced constipation. The herbal formula significantly increased spontaneous bowel movements and improved quality of life compared to placebo, with no serious adverse events.
research.periodical: Wang J, Li G, Yu Q, et al. Ma Zi Ren Wan for opioid-induced constipation in patients with cancer: a randomized controlled trial. Supportive Care in Cancer 2020; 28: 2917-2925.
